steps.title: 무슨 일 해요?
steps.scene_desc: 아침, 아파트 로비. 출근하는 지우와 커피를 든 벤이 손을 흔들며 인사
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What do you do?" (무슨 일 해요?). Goal: 하는 일을 묻고 말하기. Today's scene: 아침, 아파트 로비. 출근하는 지우와 커피를 든 벤이 손을 흔들며 인사. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What do you do?".

steps.when: 처음 만난 사람이나 아직 잘 모르는 사람에게 하는 일을 물을 때 써요.
steps.extra: ‘What are you doing?’(지금 뭐 하고 있어요?)과는 달라요.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What do you do?" (무슨 일 해요?). When to use it: 처음 만난 사람이나 아직 잘 모르는 사람에게 하는 일을 물을 때 써요. Note: ‘What are you doing?’(지금 뭐 하고 있어요?)과는 달라요.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’m a ___.".

steps.when: 내 직업을 말할 때 써요. 직업 앞에 *a*를 붙여요.
steps.extra: I’m a nurse. · 모음 소리로 시작하면 *an*: I’m an office worker.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’m a ___." (저는 ~예요.). When to use it: 내 직업을 말할 때 써요. 직업 앞에 a를 붙여요. Note: I’m a nurse. · 모음 소리로 시작하면 an: I’m an office worker.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I work at a ___.".

steps.extra: I work at a bank. · I work at a hospital.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I work at a ___." (~에서 일해요.). When to use it: 일하는 곳을 말할 때 써요. Note: I work at a bank. · I work at a hospital.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Off to Work · 아침, 아파트 로비에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Off to Work · 아침, 아파트 로비에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Ben: "Morning, Jiwoo! Off to work?" (좋은 아침이에요, 지우 씨! 출근해요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Hi, Ben! Yes. I’m late again!" (안녕하세요, 벤! 네. 오늘도 늦었어요!)
3. Ben: "No worries. Hey, Jiwoo. What do you do?" (괜찮아요. 참, 지우 씨. 무슨 일 해요?)
4. Jiwoo: "I’m a web designer. I work at a small company." (웹 디자이너예요. 작은 회사에서 일해요.)
5. Ben: "Oh, cool. Do you like your job?" (오, 멋지네요. 일은 마음에 들어요?)
6. Jiwoo: "Yes, it’s fun. I work on a computer all day. What about you?" (네, 재미있어요. 하루 종일 컴퓨터로 일해요. 벤은요?)
7. Ben: "I’m a teacher. I teach English classes at a language school." (저는 선생님이에요. 어학원에서 영어 수업을 해요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Really? Grace is a teacher, too!" (정말요? 그레이스도 선생님이잖아요!)
9. Ben: "Yep. We work at the same school." (네. 우리 같은 학원에서 일해요.)
10. Jiwoo: "That sounds interesting." (재미있겠네요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Oh, my bus! See you later, Ben!" (앗, 제 버스! 이따 봐요, 벤!)
12. Ben: "See ya!" (또 봐요!(친근한 말))
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:

1. Ben (you): "Morning, Jiwoo! Off to work?" (좋은 아침이에요, 지우 씨! 출근해요?)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Hi, Ben! Yes. I’m late again!" (안녕하세요, 벤! 네. 오늘도 늦었어요!)
3. Ben (you): "No worries. Hey, Jiwoo. What do you do?" (괜찮아요. 참, 지우 씨. 무슨 일 해요?)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "I’m a web designer. I work at a small company." (웹 디자이너예요. 작은 회사에서 일해요.)
5. Ben (you): "Oh, cool. Do you like your job?" (오, 멋지네요. 일은 마음에 들어요?)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "Yes, it’s fun. I work on a computer all day. What about you?" (네, 재미있어요. 하루 종일 컴퓨터로 일해요. 벤은요?)
7. Ben (you): "I’m a teacher. I teach English classes at a language school." (저는 선생님이에요. 어학원에서 영어 수업을 해요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "Really? Grace is a teacher, too!" (정말요? 그레이스도 선생님이잖아요!)
9. Ben (you): "Yep. We work at the same school." (네. 우리 같은 학원에서 일해요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "That sounds interesting." (재미있겠네요.)
11. Jiwoo (learner): "Oh, my bus! See you later, Ben!" (앗, 제 버스! 이따 봐요, 벤!)
12. Ben (you): "See ya!" (또 봐요!(친근한 말))
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Ben. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I’m a/an ___. I work at a ___.
head: 직업 (I’m a/an …)
일하는 곳 (I work at a …)
이렇게 말해요
rows: I’m a nurse. I work at a hospital.
I’m a teacher. I work at a school.
I’m an office worker. I work at a company.
I’m a cook. I work at a restaurant.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What do you do? / I’m a/an ___. I work at a ___. Table (직업 (I’m a/an …) → 일하는 곳 (I work at a …)):
- nurse 간호사 → hospital 병원
- teacher 선생님 → school 학교
- office worker 회사원 → company 회사
- cook 요리사 → restaurant 식당
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
지금 이 순간이 아니라 *평소에* 하는 일은 동사를 그대로 써요.
*I work* at a bank. 저는 은행에서 일해요.
*I teach* English. 저는 영어를 가르쳐요.
‘지금 하고 있는 일’은 Book 2 Lesson 4에서 배워요.

직업 하나를 말할 땐 앞에 *a*를 붙여요.
첫 *소리*가 모음(아·에·이·오·어)이면 *an*.
a teacher · a nurse · a doctor
an office worker · an engineer · an English teacher
errors: am과 work를 함께 쓰지 않아요. ‘일해요’는 work 하나로 충분해요.
틀린 문장은 아니지만 다른 질문이에요. ‘doing’은 “지금 뭐 해요?”, 직업은 do로 물어요.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 늘 하는 일은 현재형: 지금 이 순간이 아니라 평소에 하는 일은 동사를 그대로 써요. / I work at a bank. 저는 은행에서 일해요. / I teach English. 저는 영어를 가르쳐요. / ‘지금 하고 있는 일’은 Book 2 Lesson 4에서 배워요.
- a 와 an: 직업 하나를 말할 땐 앞에 a를 붙여요. / 첫 소리가 모음(아·에·이·오·어)이면 an. / a teacher · a nurse · a doctor / an office worker · an engineer · an English teacher
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m teacher. → I’m a teacher. (직업 앞에 a/an을 빼지 않아요.)
- I’m work at a bank. → I work at a bank. (am과 work를 함께 쓰지 않아요. ‘일해요’는 work 하나로 충분해요.)
- I’m a office worker. → I’m an office worker. (office는 ‘오’ 소리로 시작해서 an.)
- What are you doing? → What do you do? (틀린 문장은 아니지만 다른 질문이에요. ‘doing’은 “지금 뭐 해요?”, 직업은 do로 물어요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

I’m work at a bank. → I work at a bank.
I’m a office worker. → I’m an office worker.
What are you doing? → What do you do?

steps.note: 예) doctor / hospital → I’m a doctor. I work at a hospital. · 선생님이 그림 카드를 보여 주면 바로 문장으로 말해요.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) doctor / hospital → I’m a doctor. I work at a hospital. · 선생님이 그림 카드를 보여 주면 바로 문장으로 말해요. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: doctor → hospital | driver → bus company | engineer → car company | lawyer → law firm.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "What do you do?" (무슨 일 해요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What do you do?" / "I’m a ___." / "I work at a ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I work for a small company.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 내 일 말하기: "I’m an office worker." (회사원이에요., 보통); "I work for a small company." (작은 회사에 다녀요., 보통); "I’m a student." (학생이에요., 보통); "I’m between jobs right now." (지금은 다음 일을 구하는 중이에요., 정중)
- 묻고 이어 가기: "What about you?" (당신은요?, 친근); "Do you like your job?" (일은 마음에 들어요?, 보통)
- 대답하고 반응하기: "Yes, it’s fun." (네, 재미있어요., 친근); "It’s a lot of work." (일이 많아요., 보통); "That sounds interesting." (재미있겠네요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: at 과 for

*at* + 일하는 장소 — I work at a bank.
*for* + 회사·사람 — I work for a small company.
둘 다 ‘~에서 일해요’지만 for는 ‘그 회사 소속’이라는 느낌이에요.
일을 안 할 때는?

I’m a student. 학생이에요.
I’m between jobs. 지금은 다음 일을 구하는 중이에요.(단순한 휴식·휴가와는 달라요)
I’m retired. 은퇴했어요.
꼭 직업이 없어도 대답할 수 있어요.
steps.blank:
A: What do you do?   B: I’m ___ office worker. I work ___ a bank.
A: Do you like your job?   B: Yes, it’s fun. ___ about you?

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- at 과 for: at + 일하는 장소 — I work at a bank. / for + 회사·사람 — I work for a small company. / 둘 다 ‘~에서 일해요’지만 for는 ‘그 회사 소속’이라는 느낌이에요.
- 일을 안 할 때는?: I’m a student. 학생이에요. / I’m between jobs. 지금은 다음 일을 구하는 중이에요.(단순한 휴식·휴가와는 달라요) / I’m retired. 은퇴했어요. / 꼭 직업이 없어도 대답할 수 있어요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What do you do? B: I’m ___ office worker. I work ___ a bank. / A: Do you like your job? B: Yes, it’s fun. ___ about you? / 낱말 상자: an · at · What
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: teacher (선생님), nurse (간호사), doctor (의사), driver (운전기사), office worker (회사원), student (학생), lawyer (변호사), cook (요리사), school (학교), hospital (병원), bank (은행), office (사무실).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: job (일, 직업) — "I like my job."; work (일하다, 일) — "I work at a bank."; company (회사) — "a small company"; worker (일하는 사람) — "an office worker"; class (수업) — "an English class"; computer (컴퓨터) — "I work on a computer."; interesting (재미있는, 흥미로운) — "That sounds interesting."; hard (힘든; 열심히) — "It’s hard work."; part (부분) — "a part-time job 시간제 일".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

items: What kind of place do you work at?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What do you do?" (hint on screen: I’m a/an ___. / I’m a student.)
- "What kind of place do you work at?" (hint on screen: I work at ___. (an office · a school · a store))
- "Do you like your job?" (hint on screen: Yes, it’s fun. / It’s okay. / It’s a lot of work.)
- "Is your job hard?" (hint on screen: Yes, it’s hard. / No, it’s easy. / Sometimes.)
- "What job is interesting to you?" (hint on screen: I think ___ is interesting.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Ben’s Evening Class
steps.text: Ben is an English teacher. He teaches at a language school in Seoul. His class starts at seven in the evening. There are many different workers in his class, *such as* nurses, cooks, and lawyers. They come to class after work. They are often tired, but they work hard. In the first class, people *tend to* ask, “What do you do?” Ben likes this question. It is a good way to start.
steps.gloss: such as ~ 같은 · tend to 대개 ~하는 편이다 · language school 어학원 · after work 퇴근 후 · start 시작하다
questions: When does Ben’s class start?
What jobs do his students have?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Ben’s Evening Class". Text: "Ben is an English teacher. He teaches at a language school in Seoul. His class starts at seven in the evening. There are many different workers in his class, such as nurses, cooks, and lawyers. They come to class after work. They are often tired, but they work hard. In the first class, people tend to ask, “What do you do?” Ben likes this question. It is a good way to start." Words: such as ~ 같은 · tend to 대개 ~하는 편이다 · language school 어학원 · after work 퇴근 후 · start 시작하다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "When does Ben’s class start?" / "What jobs do his students have?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What do you do?’로 하는 일을 물을 수 있어요.
‘I’m a/an ___.’으로 내 일을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I work at a ___.’로 일하는 곳을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What do you do?’로 하는 일을 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I’m a/an ___.’으로 내 일을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I work at a ___.’로 일하는 곳을 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 아침 일과

steps.title: 아침 일과
steps.title_en: What time do you get up?
steps.goal: 일어나는 시간과 아침에 보통 하는 일 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 아침 7시 반, 아파트 엘리베이터 앞. 산책을 마치고 돌아온 운동복 차림의 그레이스와 막 나온 졸린 얼굴의 지우
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What time do you get up?" (아침 일과). Goal: 일어나는 시간과 아침에 보통 하는 일 말하기. Today's scene: 아침 7시 반, 아파트 엘리베이터 앞. 산책을 마치고 돌아온 운동복 차림의 그레이스와 막 나온 졸린 얼굴의 지우. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What time do you get up?".

steps.en: What time do you get up?
steps.when: 아침에 일어나는 시간을 물을 때 써요.
steps.extra: 대답: I get up at seven.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What time do you get up?" (몇 시에 일어나요?). When to use it: 아침에 일어나는 시간을 물을 때 써요. Note: 대답: I get up at seven.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I get up at ___.".

steps.extra: I get up at 6:30. (six thirty)
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I get up at ___." (~시에 일어나요.). When to use it: 일어나는 시간을 말해요. 시각 앞에 at. Note: I get up at 6:30. (six thirty).
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I usually ___.".

steps.when: 대부분의 경우에 하는 일을 말해요. 매번 하는 것은 아니에요.
steps.extra: I usually take a shower. · I usually walk.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I usually ___." (보통 ~해요.). When to use it: 대부분의 경우에 하는 일을 말해요. 매번 하는 것은 아니에요. Note: I usually take a shower. · I usually walk.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Morning People · 아침, 엘리베이터 앞에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Morning People · 아침, 엘리베이터 앞에서

lines.en: Good morning, Jiwoo! You look sleepy.
lines.ko: 좋은 아침이에요, 지우 씨! 졸려 보여요.

lines.en: Morning, Grace. I’m not a morning person.

lines.en: {{What time do you get up}}?
{{I get up at}} seven thirty. And you?
At six. I walk for at least thirty minutes.
Every day?
Not on weekends. Then I get back home and have breakfast.
lines.ko: 주말엔 안 해요. 그리고 집에 돌아와서 아침을 먹어요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Morning People · 아침, 엘리베이터 앞에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:

4. Jiwoo: "I get up at seven thirty. And you?" (7시 반에 일어나요. 그레이스는요?)
5. Grace: "At six. I walk for at least thirty minutes." (6시요. 적어도 30분은 걸어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Every day?" (매일요?)
7. Grace: "Not on weekends. Then I get back home and have breakfast." (주말엔 안 해요. 그리고 집에 돌아와서 아침을 먹어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "I never eat breakfast. I usually take a shower and get dressed. That’s all." (저는 아침을 안 먹어요. 보통 샤워하고 옷 입어요. 그게 다예요.)
9. Grace: "Hmm. Take your time in the morning. Eat a banana!" (음. 아침엔 서두르지 말고요. 바나나라도 먹어요!)
10. Jiwoo: "Okay! Oh no, I leave home at eight. See you!" (알겠어요! 앗, 8시에 나가야 해요. 또 봐요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

6. Jiwoo (learner): "Every day?" (매일요?)

8. Jiwoo (learner): "I never eat breakfast. I usually take a shower and get dressed. That’s all." (저는 아침을 안 먹어요. 보통 샤워하고 옷 입어요. 그게 다예요.)

Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. Grace gets up at six.
2. Grace walks every day.
3. Jiwoo always eats breakfast.
The scene they are about:
1. Grace: "Good morning, Jiwoo! You look sleepy." (좋은 아침이에요, 지우 씨! 졸려 보여요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Morning, Grace. I’m not a morning person." (안녕하세요, 그레이스. 저는 아침형 인간이 아니에요.)

4. Jiwoo: "I get up at seven thirty. And you?" (7시 반에 일어나요. 그레이스는요?)
5. Grace: "At six. I walk for at least thirty minutes." (6시요. 적어도 30분은 걸어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Every day?" (매일요?)

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: What time do you get up?
I get up at ___. I usually ___.
head: 얼마나 자주
느낌
이렇게 말해요
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What time do you get up? / I get up at ___. I usually ___. Table (얼마나 자주 → 느낌):
- always 늘 → 매번
- usually 보통 → 대부분
- sometimes 가끔 → 가끔
- never 절대 안 → 한 번도 안
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
always·usually·never는 *동사 앞*에 와요.
I *usually* get up at seven.
I *never* eat breakfast.
be동사가 있으면 그 뒤: I’m *always* tired.

‘~시에’는 *at*.
I get up *at* 7:30. (seven thirty)
I leave home *at* eight.
주말에는 on: on weekends
errors: I usually gets up at seven.
I usually get up at seven.
I 뒤 동사에는 s를 붙이지 않아요.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 빈도 낱말의 자리: always·usually·never는 동사 앞에 와요. / I usually get up at seven. / I never eat breakfast. / be동사가 있으면 그 뒤: I’m always tired.
- at + 시각: ‘~시에’는 at. / I get up at 7:30. (seven thirty) / I leave home at eight. / 주말에는 on: on weekends
Common mistakes on screen:
- I get up seven. → I get up at seven. (시각 앞에 at을 넣어요.)
- I usually gets up at seven. → I usually get up at seven. (I 뒤 동사에는 s를 붙이지 않아요.)
- I never don’t eat breakfast. → I never eat breakfast. (never에 이미 ‘안’ 뜻이 있어요.)
- I take shower. → I take a shower. (shower 앞에 a를 넣어요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

at + 시각: ‘~시에’는 at.I get up at 7:30. (seven thirty)I leave home at eight.주말에는 on: on weekends

steps.note: 예) get up / 6:30 → I usually get up at six thirty.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) get up / 6:30 → I usually get up at six thirty. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: get up → 6:30 | leave home → 8:00 | take a shower → 7:00 | have breakfast → 7:20.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: What time do you get up?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "What time do you get up?" (아침 일과); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What time do you get up?" / "I get up at ___." / "I usually ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 아침에 하는 일: "I always have breakfast." (늘 아침을 먹어요., 보통); "I take a shower." (샤워해요., 보통); "I brush my teeth." (이를 닦아요., 보통); "I get dressed." (옷을 입어요., 보통)
- 시간 말하기: "I leave home at ___." (~시에 집을 나서요., 보통); "I never eat breakfast." (아침은 절대 안 먹어요., 보통)
- 묻고 대답하기: "Every day?" (매일요?, 친근); "Not on weekends." (주말엔 안 해요., 보통); "I’m not a morning person." (저는 아침형 인간이 아니에요., 친근)

Word list on screen: often (자주) — "I often walk."; every (매 ~, ~마다) — "every day"; person (사람) — "a morning person"; typical (평소의, 보통의) — "a typical day"; weekly (매주의) — "a weekly class"; breakfast (아침 식사) — "have breakfast"; walk (걷다) — "I walk for thirty minutes."; late (늦게) — "I sometimes get up late."; sleepy (졸린) — "You look sleepy.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:

steps.title: Grace’s Morning
steps.text: Grace gets up at six on weekdays. Her morning routine is simple. First, she walks in the park for *at least* thirty minutes. She *gets back* home at seven. Then she has breakfast. Her first class *takes place* at ten, so she has time. *However*, on weekends she sleeps late. Today Jiwoo *finds out* about Grace’s morning. “Six? Wow!” she says.
steps.gloss: simple 간단한 · at least 적어도 · get back 돌아오다 · take place (일이) 열리다 · however 하지만 · find out 알게 되다

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What time does Grace get back home?" / "When does her first class take place?". steps.title: 어떻게 가요?
steps.title_en: How do you get to work?
steps.scene_desc: 아침, 동네 버스 정류장. 지우와 백팩을 멘 대니얼이 버스를 기다리고, 앞 도로는 차로 꽉 막힘
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "How do you get to work?" (어떻게 가요?). Goal: 가는 방법과 걸리는 시간 말하기. Today's scene: 아침, 동네 버스 정류장. 지우와 백팩을 멘 대니얼이 버스를 기다리고, 앞 도로는 차로 꽉 막힘. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "How do you get to ___?".

steps.extra: How do you get to work? · How do you get to school?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "How do you get to ___?" (~에 어떻게 가요?). When to use it: 가는 방법을 물어요. Note: How do you get to work? · How do you get to school?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I go by ___. / I walk.".

steps.title: At the Bus Stop · 아침, 버스 정류장에서

lines.en: Hi, Jiwoo! Waiting for the bus?
Yes. {{How do you get to}} school, Daniel?
{{I go by}} subway. And you?
I take the bus. {{It takes}} forty {{minutes}}.
Forty? Why?
The traffic is terrible. Look!
Is your office far?
No, it’s not far. About three miles.
Then take the subway with me. I get off at City Hall.

lines.en: Really? How long does it take?

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "At the Bus Stop · 아침, 버스 정류장에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "Hi, Jiwoo! Waiting for the bus?" (안녕, 지우! 버스 기다려요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Yes. How do you get to school, Daniel?" (네. 대니얼은 학교에 어떻게 가요?)
3. Daniel: "I go by subway. And you?" (지하철로 가요. 지우는요?)
4. Jiwoo: "I take the bus. It takes forty minutes." (버스 타요. 40분 걸려요.)
5. Daniel: "Forty? Why?" (40분이요? 왜요?)
6. Jiwoo: "The traffic is terrible. Look!" (차가 엄청 막혀요. 봐요!)
7. Daniel: "Is your office far?" (회사가 멀어요?)
8. Jiwoo: "No, it’s not far. About three miles." (아뇨, 안 멀어요. 3마일(5km)쯤이에요.)
9. Daniel: "Then take the subway with me. I get off at City Hall." (그럼 저랑 지하철 타요. 저는 시청에서 내려요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Really? How long does it take?" (정말요? 얼마나 걸려요?)
11. Daniel: "About twenty minutes." (20분쯤요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Okay. Let’s go!" (좋아요. 가요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.

Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.

Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I go by ___. / I walk. It takes ___ minutes.
head: 어떻게
얼마나
이렇게 말해요
rows: I go by bus. It takes thirty minutes.
I go by subway. It takes twenty minutes.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: How do you get to ___? / I go by ___. / I walk. It takes ___ minutes. Table (어떻게 → 얼마나):
- bus 버스 → 30분
- subway 지하철 → 20분
- car 차 → 15분
- walk 걷기 → 10분
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*by* bus · *by* subway · *by* car · *by* bike
by 뒤에는 a·the 없이 써요.
걸어갈 땐 I *walk*. (= on foot)

‘~ 걸려요’는 *It takes*.
It takes twenty minutes. 20분 걸려요.
How long does it take? 얼마나 걸려요?
errors: 걸어갈 땐 I walk. 또는 on foot.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- by + 교통수단: by bus · by subway · by car · by bike / by 뒤에는 a·the 없이 써요. / 걸어갈 땐 I walk. (= on foot)
- It takes + 시간: ‘~ 걸려요’는 It takes. / It takes twenty minutes. 20분 걸려요. / How long does it take? 얼마나 걸려요?
Common mistakes on screen:
- I go by a bus. → I go by bus. (by 뒤에는 a를 넣지 않아요.)
- I go by walk. → I walk. (걸어갈 땐 I walk. 또는 on foot.)
- It takes twenty minute. → It takes twenty minutes. (둘 이상이면 minutes.)
- How long it takes? → How long does it take? (물을 때는 does를 넣어요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

I go by walk. → I walk.

steps.note: 예) subway / 25 → I go by subway. It takes twenty-five minutes.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) subway / 25 → I go by subway. It takes twenty-five minutes. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: subway → 25 | bus → 40 | bike → 15 | taxi → 10.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "How do you get to work?" (어떻게 가요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "How do you get to ___?" / "I go by ___. / I walk." / "It takes ___ minutes.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 교통수단 말하기: "I take the subway." (지하철을 타요., 보통); "I take the bus." (버스를 타요., 보통); "I drive to work." (차로 출근해요., 보통); "I get off at ___." (~에서 내려요., 보통)
- 시간·거리 묻기: "How long does it take?" (얼마나 걸려요?, 보통); "About twenty minutes." (20분쯤요., 보통); "Is it far?" (멀어요?, 보통); "It’s not far." (멀지 않아요., 보통)

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:

Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.

Picture words on screen. New: bus (버스), subway (지하철), train (기차), taxi (택시), car (차), truck (트럭), van (승합차), bike (자전거), traffic (교통(량)), stop (정류장), station (역). Review words: walk (걷다).

Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.

Word list on screen: take (타다; (시간이) 걸리다) — "take the bus"; far (먼) — "Is it far?"; close (가까운) — "It’s close."; about (약, ~쯤) — "about ten minutes"; long (긴, 오래) — "How long does it take?"; mile (마일(약 1.6km)) — "three miles"; transportation (교통수단) — "public transportation 대중교통"; drive (운전하다) — "I drive to work."; difficult (어려운) — "Parking is difficult.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "How do you get to work or school?" (hint on screen: I go by ___. / I walk. · 어디인지는 말하지 않아도 돼요.)

- "Is it far?" (hint on screen: Yes, it’s far. / No, it’s not far.)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Daniel’s Bike
steps.text: Daniel usually goes to school by subway. It takes twenty minutes. But today the subway is late *due to* a problem. So he takes a bike from the bike station. It’s *such a* nice day! Later, he sends Jiwoo a photo. In the photo, he *points out* a new café on the way. “*Perhaps* we can try it this weekend!” he says.
steps.gloss: due to ~ 때문에 · such a 정말 ~한 · point out 가리키다, 짚어 주다 · perhaps 아마 · on the way 가는 길에
questions: Why is the subway late?
How does Daniel go to school today?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Daniel’s Bike". Text: "Daniel usually goes to school by subway. It takes twenty minutes. But today the subway is late due to a problem. So he takes a bike from the bike station. It’s such a nice day! Later, he sends Jiwoo a photo. In the photo, he points out a new café on the way. “Perhaps we can try it this weekend!” he says." Words: due to ~ 때문에 · such a 정말 ~한 · point out 가리키다, 짚어 주다 · perhaps 아마 · on the way 가는 길에.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why is the subway late?" / "How does Daniel go to school today?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 지금 뭐 해요?
steps.scene_desc: 토요일 낮, 영상 통화 화면 둘로 나뉨. 왼쪽: 지우가 집 부엌에서 프라이팬으로 볶음밥을 만들며 휴대폰을 봄. 오른쪽: 클로이가 카페에서 노트북 옆에 커피를 두고 손을 흔듦
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What are you doing?" (지금 뭐 해요?). Goal: 지금 하는 일을 말하기. Today's scene: 토요일 낮, 영상 통화 화면 둘로 나뉨. 왼쪽: 지우가 집 부엌에서 프라이팬으로 볶음밥을 만들며 휴대폰을 봄. 오른쪽: 클로이가 카페에서 노트북 옆에 커피를 두고 손을 흔듦. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What are you doing?".

steps.when: 지금 이 순간 하는 일을 물어요.
steps.extra: ‘What do you do?’(무슨 일 해요?)와 달라요.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What are you doing?" (지금 뭐 해요?). When to use it: 지금 이 순간 하는 일을 물어요. Note: ‘What do you do?’(무슨 일 해요?)와 달라요.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’m ___ing.".

steps.extra: I’m cooking lunch. · I’m watching TV.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’m ___ing." (~하고 있어요.). When to use it: 지금 하는 일을 말해요. Note: I’m cooking lunch. · I’m watching TV.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’m busy right now.".

steps.extra: I’m busy right now. Can I call you later?
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’m busy right now." (지금 바빠요.). When to use it: 지금은 이야기하기 어렵다고 말해요. Note: I’m busy right now. Can I call you later?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Video Call · 토요일 낮, 영상 통화") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 동사
-ing
이렇게 말해요
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What are you doing? / I’m ___ing. / I’m busy right now. Table (동사 → -ing):
- cook → cooking
- watch → watching
- wait → waiting
- take → taking
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I *am* cook*ing*. 지금 요리하고 있어요.
She *is* work*ing*. · They *are* relax*ing*.
평소 하는 일은 현재형(Book 2 Lesson 1): I work at a bank.

*Are* you working now?
— Yes, I am. / No, I’m not.
I’m *not* working right now.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 지금 하는 일: am/is/are + -ing: I am cooking. 지금 요리하고 있어요. / She is working. · They are relaxing. / 평소 하는 일은 현재형(Book 2 Lesson 1): I work at a bank.
- 물을 때·아닐 때: Are you working now? / — Yes, I am. / No, I’m not. / I’m not working right now.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I cooking dinner. → I’m cooking dinner. (am(’m)을 빼지 않아요.)
- I’m cook dinner. → I’m cooking dinner. (am 뒤에는 -ing.)
- Are you work now? → Are you working now? (be동사 뒤에는 -ing.)
- I’m siting on the sofa. → I’m sitting on the sofa. (sit은 t를 하나 더: sitting.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 지금 하는 일: am/is/are + -ing: I am cooking. 지금 요리하고 있어요.She is working. · They are relaxing.평소 하는 일은 현재형(Book 2 Lesson 1): I work at a bank.
물을 때·아닐 때: Are you working now?— Yes, I am. / No, I’m not.I’m not working right now.

steps.note: 예) watch / TV → What are you doing? — I’m watching TV.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) watch / TV → What are you doing? — I’m watching TV. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: watch → TV | wait for → the bus | look for → my keys | take → a nap.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "What are you doing?" (지금 뭐 해요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What are you doing?" / "I’m ___ing." / "I’m busy right now.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 지금 하는 일: "I’m cooking dinner." (저녁 만들고 있어요., 보통); "I’m watching TV." (TV 보고 있어요., 보통); "I’m waiting for the bus." (버스 기다리고 있어요., 보통); "I’m looking for my keys." (열쇠 찾고 있어요., 보통)
- 전화로 묻기: "Is it a bad time?" (지금 곤란해요?, 보통); "Are you working now?" (지금 일하고 있어요?, 보통); "Not right now." (지금은 아니에요., 보통)
- 대답하기: "I’m just relaxing." (그냥 쉬고 있어요., 친근); "I’m on my way." (가는 중이에요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: ‘지금’을 나타내는 말

now · right now 지금 · at the moment 지금 이 순간
*still* 아직도 — I’m still working.
*just* 그냥 — I’m just relaxing.
-ing 만들기

cook → cooking 대부분 + ing
relax → relaxing · take → tak*ing*(e 빼고)
sit → sit*t*ing(자음 하나 더)
steps.blank:
A: What ___ you doing?   B: I’m ___ dinner.
A: Is it a bad ___?   B: No, I’m just ___.
낱말 상자: are · cooking · time · relaxing
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- ‘지금’을 나타내는 말: now · right now 지금 · at the moment 지금 이 순간 / still 아직도 — I’m still working. / just 그냥 — I’m just relaxing.
- -ing 만들기: cook → cooking 대부분 + ing / relax → relaxing · take → taking(e 빼고) / sit → sitting(자음 하나 더)
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What ___ you doing? B: I’m ___ dinner. / A: Is it a bad ___? B: No, I’m just ___. / 낱말 상자: are · cooking · time · relaxing
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: relaxing (쉬는 중), TV (텔레비전), nap (낮잠), email (이메일), video call (영상 통화), lunch break (점심시간), errand (볼일, 심부름), cooking (요리하는 중), watching (보는 중), waiting (기다리는 중), looking for (찾는 중), working (일하는 중).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: moment (순간) — "at the moment"; just (그냥, 막) — "I’m just relaxing."; still (아직도) — "I’m still waiting."; now (지금) — "right now"; right (바로) — "right now"; way (길) — "I’m on my way."; call (전화하다) — "Call me later.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What are you doing right now?
Yes, I am. / Not right now.
What do you usually do on your lunch break?
I call you at a bad time. What do you say?
Sorry, I’m busy right now. Can I call you later?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What are you doing right now?" (hint on screen: I’m ___ing.)
- "Are you working right now?" (hint on screen: Yes, I am. / Not right now.)
- "What do you usually do on your lunch break?" (hint on screen: I usually ___. (평소 일은 현재형))
- "I call you at a bad time. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Sorry, I’m busy right now. Can I call you later?)
- "Ask me what I’m doing." (hint on screen: What are you doing?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: What are you doing right now?
Are you working right now?
What do you usually do on your lunch break?

steps.title: Chloe’s Saturday
steps.text: It’s Saturday afternoon. Chloe is at a café. She is *looking up* a recipe for dinner. The recipe *calls for* fish, lemon, and rice. Her boss *is likely to* send an email later, so she checks her phone. She works *up to* two hours on weekends, no more. Right now, she is just relaxing. Then she calls Jiwoo. Jiwoo is cooking lunch!
steps.gloss: look up 찾아보다 · recipe 요리법 · call for 필요로 하다 · be likely to ~할 것 같다 · up to 최대 ~까지
questions: What is Chloe looking up?
What does the recipe call for?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Chloe’s Saturday". Text: "It’s Saturday afternoon. Chloe is at a café. She is looking up a recipe for dinner. The recipe calls for fish, lemon, and rice. Her boss is likely to send an email later, so she checks her phone. She works up to two hours on weekends, no more. Right now, she is just relaxing. Then she calls Jiwoo. Jiwoo is cooking lunch!" Words: look up 찾아보다 · recipe 요리법 · call for 필요로 하다 · be likely to ~할 것 같다 · up to 최대 ~까지.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What is Chloe looking up?" / "What does the recipe call for?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What are you doing?’로 지금 하는 일을 물을 수 있어요.
‘I’m ___ing.’로 지금 하는 일을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I’m busy right now.’로 지금 바쁘다고 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What are you doing?’로 지금 하는 일을 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I’m ___ing.’로 지금 하는 일을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’m busy right now.’로 지금 바쁘다고 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 식당에서 주문
steps.scene_desc: 저녁, 동네 작은 식당 창가 자리. 그레이스와 지우가 메뉴판을 보고, 앞치마를 한 직원(조연)이 주문을 받음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Are you ready to order?" (식당에서 주문). Goal: 식당에서 주문하고 계산 요청하기. Today's scene: 저녁, 동네 작은 식당 창가 자리. 그레이스와 지우가 메뉴판을 보고, 앞치마를 한 직원(조연)이 주문을 받음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Are you ready to order?".

steps.when: 식당 직원이 주문을 받을 때 써요.
steps.extra: 대답: Yes, I’d like ___. / Not yet.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Are you ready to order?" (주문하시겠어요?). When to use it: 식당 직원이 주문을 받을 때 써요. Note: 대답: Yes, I’d like ___. / Not yet.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’d like the ___, please.".

steps.when: 공손하게 주문해요. I’d like = I would like.
steps.extra: I’d like the soup, please.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’d like the ___, please." (~ 주세요.). When to use it: 공손하게 주문해요. I’d like = I would like. Note: I’d like the soup, please.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Can I get the check, please?".

steps.en: Can I get the check, please?
steps.extra: check(미국) = bill
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "Can I get the check, please?" (계산서 주시겠어요?). When to use it: 다 먹고 계산할 때 써요. Note: check(미국) = bill.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Dinner Out · 저녁, 동네 식당에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Dinner Out · 저녁, 동네 식당에서

lines.en: Hi. A table for two, please.
Sure. Here’s the menu.
Everything looks good. What do you recommend?
The tomato soup is great. {{Are you ready to order}}?
Yes. {{I’d like the}} tomato soup, {{please}}.
I’ll have the same. Is it spicy?
No, it’s not spicy. Anything to drink?
Can I get some water?
Everything was great! {{Can I get the check, please}}?
Let’s split the bill.
Okay. Thanks, Grace!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Dinner Out · 저녁, 동네 식당에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Jiwoo: "Hi. A table for two, please." (안녕하세요. 두 명이요.)
2. Staff: "Sure. Here’s the menu." (네. 여기 메뉴요.)
3. Grace: "Everything looks good. What do you recommend?" (다 맛있어 보이네요. 뭐가 좋아요?)
4. Staff: "The tomato soup is great. Are you ready to order?" (토마토 수프가 맛있어요. 주문하시겠어요?)
5. Jiwoo: "Yes. I’d like the tomato soup, please." (네. 토마토 수프 주세요.)
6. Grace: "I’ll have the same. Is it spicy?" (저도 같은 걸로요. 매워요?)
7. Staff: "No, it’s not spicy. Anything to drink?" (아뇨, 안 매워요. 마실 건요?)
8. Grace: "Can I get some water?" (물 좀 주시겠어요?)
9. Jiwoo: "Everything was great! Can I get the check, please?" (다 맛있었어요! 계산서 주시겠어요?)
10. Grace: "Let’s split the bill." (나눠서 내요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Okay. Thanks, Grace!" (좋아요. 고마워요, 그레이스!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

1. Jiwoo (learner): "Hi. A table for two, please." (안녕하세요. 두 명이요.)
2. Staff (you): "Sure. Here’s the menu." (네. 여기 메뉴요.)

4. Staff (you): "The tomato soup is great. Are you ready to order?" (토마토 수프가 맛있어요. 주문하시겠어요?)
5. Jiwoo (learner): "Yes. I’d like the tomato soup, please." (네. 토마토 수프 주세요.)
6. Grace (you): "I’ll have the same. Is it spicy?" (저도 같은 걸로요. 매워요?)
7. Staff (you): "No, it’s not spicy. Anything to drink?" (아뇨, 안 매워요. 마실 건요?)
8. Grace (you): "Can I get some water?" (물 좀 주시겠어요?)
9. Jiwoo (learner): "Everything was great! Can I get the check, please?" (다 맛있었어요! 계산서 주시겠어요?)
10. Grace (you): "Let’s split the bill." (나눠서 내요.)
11. Jiwoo (learner): "Okay. Thanks, Grace!" (좋아요. 고마워요, 그레이스!)

Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. Jiwoo orders tomato soup.
2. Grace orders steak.
3. They split the bill.
The scene they are about:
1. Jiwoo: "Hi. A table for two, please." (안녕하세요. 두 명이요.)
2. Staff: "Sure. Here’s the menu." (네. 여기 메뉴요.)
3. Grace: "Everything looks good. What do you recommend?" (다 맛있어 보이네요. 뭐가 좋아요?)
4. Staff: "The tomato soup is great. Are you ready to order?" (토마토 수프가 맛있어요. 주문하시겠어요?)
5. Jiwoo: "Yes. I’d like the tomato soup, please." (네. 토마토 수프 주세요.)
6. Grace: "I’ll have the same. Is it spicy?" (저도 같은 걸로요. 매워요?)
7. Staff: "No, it’s not spicy. Anything to drink?" (아뇨, 안 매워요. 마실 건요?)
8. Grace: "Can I get some water?" (물 좀 주시겠어요?)
9. Jiwoo: "Everything was great! Can I get the check, please?" (다 맛있었어요! 계산서 주시겠어요?)
10. Grace: "Let’s split the bill." (나눠서 내요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Okay. Thanks, Grace!" (좋아요. 고마워요, 그레이스!)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 메뉴
이렇게 주문해요
rows: Can I see the dessert menu?
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Are you ready to order? / I’d like the ___, please. Table (메뉴 → 이렇게 주문해요):
- soup 수프 → I’d like the soup, please.
- salad 샐러드 → I’d like the salad, please.
- steak 스테이크 → I’ll have the steak, please.
- dessert 디저트 → Can I see the dessert menu?
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
‘~ 주세요’를 공손하게: *I’d like* the soup, please.
I want보다 부드러워요.
짧게: I’ll have the steak.

식당에서 달라고 할 때: *Can I get* some water?
*Can I get* the check, please? 계산서 주세요.
check(미국) = bill(영국)
errors: 문법은 맞지만 식당에서는 명령처럼 들릴 수 있어요. 더 공손하게: Can I get some water?
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I’d like = I would like: ‘~ 주세요’를 공손하게: I’d like the soup, please. / I want보다 부드러워요. / 짧게: I’ll have the steak.
- Can I get ~?: 식당에서 달라고 할 때: Can I get some water? / Can I get the check, please? 계산서 주세요. / check(미국) = bill(영국)
Common mistakes on screen:
- I like the soup, please. → I’d like the soup, please. (주문할 땐 I’d like. (I like는 ‘좋아해요’))
- I’d like soup tomato. → I’d like the tomato soup. (꾸미는 말(tomato)은 앞에.)
- I’ll have same. → I’ll have the same. (same 앞에는 the.)
- Give me water. → Can I get some water? (문법은 맞지만 식당에서는 명령처럼 들릴 수 있어요. 더 공손하게: Can I get some water?)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) soup / water → I’d like the soup, please. Can I get some water?
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) soup / water → I’d like the soup, please. Can I get some water? Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: soup → water | salad → coffee | steak → juice | pasta → tea.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Can I get the check, please?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Are you ready to order?" (식당에서 주문); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Are you ready to order?" / "I’d like the ___, please." / "Can I get the check, please?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 자리·메뉴: "A table for two, please." (두 명이요., 보통); "Can I see the menu?" (메뉴 볼 수 있어요?, 보통); "What do you recommend?" (뭐가 맛있어요?, 정중)
- 주문하기: "I’ll have the same." (같은 걸로 할게요., 보통); "Can I get some water?" (물 좀 주시겠어요?, 보통)
- 계산하기: "It’s on me." (제가 살게요., 친근); "Let’s split the bill." (나눠서 내요., 친근); "Is service included?" (봉사료 포함이에요?, 정중); "Everything was great." (다 맛있었어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:

steps.title: Dinner with Grace
steps.text: Grace and Jiwoo go to a small restaurant *in order to* have a nice dinner together. The server is kind and *points out* the soup of the day. Jiwoo orders it, and Grace has the same. Jiwoo is very hungry. She enjoys the soup. The total is forty thousand won, twenty thousand won *per* person. They split the bill.

steps.title: 이거 얼마예요?
steps.goal: 가격을 묻고 다른 색을 찾고 사기
steps.scene_desc: 동네 작은 생활용품 가게. 마야와 지우가 알록달록한 머그잔 진열대 앞에서 초록 머그잔을 들어 보고, 계산대에 직원(조연)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "How much is this mug?" (이거 얼마예요?). Goal: 가격을 묻고 다른 색을 찾고 사기. Today's scene: 동네 작은 생활용품 가게. 마야와 지우가 알록달록한 머그잔 진열대 앞에서 초록 머그잔을 들어 보고, 계산대에 직원(조연). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "How much is this ___?".

steps.extra: How much is this mug?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "How much is this ___?" (이 ~ 얼마예요?). When to use it: 가까이 있는 물건값을 물어요. Note: How much is this mug?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Do you have a ___ one?".

steps.extra: Do you have a blue one? · a small one
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Do you have a ___ one?" (~ 것도 있어요?). When to use it: 다른 색·크기를 찾아요. Note: Do you have a blue one? · a small one.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’ll take it.".

steps.extra: 여럿이면 I’ll take them.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’ll take it." (이걸로 할게요.). When to use it: 사기로 정했을 때 써요. Note: 여럿이면 I’ll take them.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: How much is this ___? / Do you have a ___ one? / I’ll take it. Table ( → 하나):
- 가까이 → How much is this mug?
- 멀리 → How much is that bag?
- 색 바꾸기 → Do you have a blue one?

Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:

먼 것 하나 *that* · 여럿 *those*
How much *are these*? 여럿이면 are.

같은 낱말을 또 말하지 않고 *one*.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- this · that · these · those: 가까운 것 하나 this · 여럿 these / 먼 것 하나 that · 여럿 those / How much are these? 여럿이면 are.
- one 으로 바꿔 말하기: 같은 낱말을 또 말하지 않고 one. / Do you have a blue one? (= a blue mug) / I’ll take the green one.
Common mistakes on screen:
- How much is these? → How much are these? (these(여럿)엔 are.)
- Do you have a blue? → Do you have a blue one? (색 뒤에 one을 넣어요.)
- I’ll take it two. → I’ll take two. (개수를 말할 땐 it을 빼요.)
- It’s too much expensive. → It’s too expensive. (too 하나로 ‘너무’예요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) mug / a red one → How much is this mug? Do you have a red one? Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: mug → a red one | bag → a black one | T-shirt → a white one | cup → a small one.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "How much is this mug?" (이거 얼마예요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "How much is this ___?" / "Do you have a ___ one?" / "I’ll take it.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
